title: What Is the Oldest Building in Europe?
description: Europe's oldest standing buildings: the Cairn of Barnenez, Malta's Ggantija temples, and Newgrange, with honest dating ranges and visiting tips.
body_html:
The short answer: the oldest standing buildings in Europe are Neolithic stone monuments, and the Cairn of Barnenez in Brittany, France, is generally considered the leading candidate, with construction beginning around 4800 BC, roughly seven thousand years ago. That makes it older than Stonehenge's stone circle and older than the Egyptian pyramids. Close behind are the megalithic temples of Malta, notably Ġgantija on the island of Gozo, and the great passage tombs of Ireland, such as Newgrange. All of these survive today and can be visited.

The longer answer is more interesting, because it depends heavily on what you mean by "building." This article walks through the definitional question honestly, profiles the main candidates with their accepted dating ranges, and ends with practical notes on seeing them in person.

What Counts as the "Oldest Building"?

Archaeologists distinguish between several claims that often get blurred in headlines:

  • Oldest structure: any human-made construction, including standing stones, earthworks, and enclosures. By this measure, sites like Göbekli Tepe in Turkey (usually dated to the 10th–9th millennium BC, and on the Asian side of the conventional Europe boundary) push the story back much further.
  • Oldest building: usually taken to mean a roofed, enclosed space you can enter. This is where the megalithic tombs and temples of Atlantic and Mediterranean Europe come in, many still have their original stone roofs.
  • Oldest building still in use: a different contest entirely. The Pantheon in Rome (2nd century AD) is often cited as the best-known ancient building in continuous use, but it is millennia younger than the Neolithic candidates.

Dating is another honest complication. Prehistoric monuments are dated by radiocarbon samples from associated material, which yields ranges rather than years, and monuments were often built, extended, and remodeled over centuries. Every date below should be read as an approximation with scholarly error bars.

The Leading Candidates

Cairn of Barnenez, Brittany, France (c. 4800 BC)

The Cairn of Barnenez is a huge dry-stone mound, over 70 meters long, containing eleven passage tombs. Radiocarbon evidence indicates the first phase was built around 4800 BC, with a second phase following centuries later. Because its chambers are roofed, enterable stone spaces, and because its dating is unusually early and well supported, Barnenez is widely cited as the oldest, or among the very oldest, buildings still standing in Europe. It is sometimes called one of the oldest buildings in the world.

The megalithic temples of Malta (c. 3600–2500 BC)

Malta and Gozo hold a remarkable cluster of freestanding stone temples, several of which are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Ġgantija on Gozo is the oldest of the group, generally dated to around 3600 BC. Others, including Ħaġar Qim, Mnajdra, and Tarxien, followed over the next millennium. The Maltese temples matter in this debate for a particular reason: they are usually described as among the world's oldest freestanding buildings, structures built up from the ground as architecture, rather than mounds containing chambers. Their curved facades, corbelled walls, and clover-leaf plans are genuinely architectural in a way that still impresses visitors.

Newgrange and the Brú na Bóinne tombs, Ireland (c. 3200 BC)

Newgrange, the most famous of the great passage tombs in Ireland's Boyne Valley, was built around 3200 BC. Its corbelled central chamber has remained intact and essentially waterproof for some five thousand years, an extraordinary feat of dry-stone engineering, and its passage is famously aligned so that the rising sun at the winter solstice penetrates to the inner chamber through a purpose-built "roof-box" opening. Its neighbors Knowth and Dowth are comparable in age and scale.

Knap of Howar, Orkney, Scotland (c. 3700–3500 BC)

A different kind of record: the Knap of Howar, on the island of Papa Westray in Orkney, consists of two conjoined dry-stone houses generally dated to around 3700–3500 BC. It is often described as the oldest preserved house in northern Europe, domestic architecture rather than a tomb or temple, with stone furniture still in place. The nearby village of Skara Brae (c. 3100 BC) is younger but even better preserved.

Other notable early monuments

  • La Hougue Bie, Jersey (c. 4000–3500 BC): a passage grave under a large mound, one of the best-preserved in western Europe.
  • Dolmen de Menga and neighbors, Antequera, Spain (4th millennium BC): massive dolmens whose capstones rank among the heaviest megaliths in Europe.
  • West Kennet Long Barrow, England (c. 3650 BC): an accessible chambered tomb near Avebury.
  • Hypogeum of Ħal Saflieni, Malta (4th–3rd millennium BC): not a building but a subterranean complex carved from rock, architecture in negative.

Why So Many Survivors Are Tombs and Temples

Survival bias shapes this entire list. Neolithic people lived mostly in timber, turf, and daub buildings that decayed within generations; they reserved megalithic stone for the dead and the sacred. Massive stones, low profiles, and covering mounds protected these monuments from weather, and their ritual importance often protected them from stone-robbing. Orkney is the exception that proves the rule: with little timber available, islanders built even their houses in stone, which is why domestic architecture survives there. The lesson recurs throughout architectural history, what a culture builds in permanent materials tells you what it valued most, a theme we explore across eras in our primer on architecture styles around the world.

Visiting the Oldest Buildings in Europe Today

All of the major candidates are open to visitors in some form:

  1. Barnenez is a managed monument in Brittany with a visitor center; you can walk the cairn's exterior and view several chambers.
  2. Ġgantija has a modern interpretive center, and Malta's other temples, Ħaġar Qim and Mnajdra, sit under protective canopies on a dramatic coastal site.
  3. Newgrange is accessible only by guided tour from the Brú na Bóinne visitor centre; demand for the solstice-morning experience is so high that places are allocated by lottery.
  4. Knap of Howar and Skara Brae reward the journey to Orkney, which has one of the densest concentrations of Neolithic monuments anywhere.

A few practical notes apply everywhere: these are fragile, protected monuments, so expect restricted access to interiors, book ahead in peak season, and check opening arrangements before traveling, several sites close chambers for conservation work with little notice. Interiors are dark, low, and uneven underfoot, and the most rewarding visits pair the monument itself with its site museum, where the excavated finds put the architecture in human context.

When you go, photograph the details, corbelling, kerbstones, megalithic art, and try running your photos through our AI architecture analyzer to unpack construction techniques. And if prehistoric architecture sparks a broader interest in how European building evolved from these beginnings through Romanesque and beyond, our style library traces the whole arc.

The deepest takeaway: "oldest" is a moving target of definitions and dating ranges, but the monuments themselves are not. Seven thousand years on, you can still stand inside a room built by some of Europe's first farmers, and that is as close to time travel as architecture gets.
